1. To meet someone on the road, by chance or while seeking: two people or groups arrive at the same place at the same time. In Genesis 32:17, Jacob prepares his servants to meet Esau, his brother, whom he fears. In 1 Samuel 25:20, Abigail descends from her donkey and meets David with his warriors coming toward her.
2. To deliberately go to meet someone: to go out to greet or speak with them. This is usually a positive, intentional action. In Exodus 4:27, Aaron goes to meet Moses in the desert.
3. To strike violently, to attack or rush upon someone: the word takes on the meaning of a hostile or dangerous collision. In Exodus 4:24, the Lord "attacks" him during the night to kill him — a terrifying encounter. Similarly, in Hosea 13:8, God promises that He will pounce on the people like a bear deprived of her cubs.
4. To mutually meet, to come toward each other: several people cross paths or gather. In Proverbs 29:13, "the poor and the oppressor meet" — two worlds that should not have approached each other find themselves face to face.
H6298.origine: The Hebrew root פגש (p-g-sh) evokes the idea of collision, of shock. It is related to Arabic, which has a similar meaning of "to collide" or "to meet violently." The word can describe both an ordinary meeting and a hostile or sudden encounter. In Hebrew, there are three forms: the simple form (Qal) for a passive or mutual meeting, the reflexive form (Niphal) for the action of meeting together, and the intensive form (Piel) for a decisive or violent meeting.
H6298.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical narratives, wisdom literature, and prophecies. In the narratives, it describes ordinary human encounters: Jacob waits to meet Esau (Genesis 32-33), David crosses paths with Abigail (1 Samuel 25), Aaron meets Moses (Exodus 4). But it also describes hostile or supernatural encounters: the Lord confronts Moses at night (Exodus 4:24), God pounces on Israel like a fierce beast (Hosea 13:8). In Wisdom literature, the word takes on an almost philosophical tone: the poor and the oppressor meet before the Creator (Proverbs 29:13), or one encounters folly and danger (Proverbs 17:12, Job 5:14).
H6298.portee: This word reminds us that our encounters are never mere chance in the eyes of God. Whether peaceful or fearsome, mundane or decisive, they are part of His plan. To meet someone is also to find oneself before a reality that confronts and transforms us — whether it be the grace of a person or the judgment of God.

sens: Pay a price to free someone from slavery or satisfy a debt
Deliver someone from danger, oppression, or the enemy
Save from the power of sin and death through a divine act
Take back or recover what belongs to someone
H6299.detail:
1. To redeem means to pay a price to free someone from slavery or obligation: it is the image of the firstborn animal that is "redeemed" with money or a lamb instead of being consecrated to the temple (Exodus 13:13). The word evokes the concrete cost of freedom.
2. To deliver means to save someone from immediate danger: it is the Lord who "delivers" the soul of His servants from oppression (Psalms 34:23) or who "delivers" the faithful from wicked men (Psalms 119:134). The image is that of a prisoner or persecuted person being snatched from the hand of their enemy.
3. To save from sin and death is the deepest spiritual meaning: God "redeemed" Israel by His great power (Nehemiah 1:10) and freed them from Egypt. The redemption here is not a commercial transaction but a sovereign act of love that restores a relationship with God.
4. To take back or recover, in the context of land or property: one who has sold their property can "redeem" it to recover it (Leviticus 27:27). The word then means to become the owner again of what had been ceded.
H6299.origine: The Hebrew root פָּדָה (padah) expresses the idea of untying, detaching, or liberating by paying a price or intervening with power. The family of the word includes forms that emphasize the action of the one who redeems (the redeemer) and the state of the one who is redeemed. This verb belongs to the vocabulary of civil law (redemption of property or persons) and gradually enriches itself with a theological meaning: God presents Himself as the one who "redeems" His people, basing His action not on a transaction but on His covenant and faithfulness.
H6299.emploi: The verb "redeem" appears 48 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the Psalms. In the Mosaic period, it designates the legal obligation to redeem the firstborn unclean animal, the Hebrew servant, or a sold property (Exodus 13:13; Leviticus 27:27). In historical narratives, the word applies to the deliverance of an individual in peril or a threatened tribe (2 Samuel 4:9; 1 Samuel 14:45). But its richest usage is found in the Psalms and the Prophets: God "redeems" Israel from Egyptian slavery, snatches them from oppression, saves them from death. This transition from the concrete to the spiritual shows that redemption ultimately becomes the expression of the definitive deliverance of the people by divine power and grace.
H6299.portee: For the believer reading this word, "redeem" reveals that God does not look on from afar: He actively intervenes to free His people. He is not a distant God, but a God who pays the price, who turns away from evil, who breaks the chains. Redemption also shows that our freedom has a cost and value in the eyes of God — we are not saved without a price, but by the sovereign power and faithful love of the Lord. This image prepares the heart to understand the ultimate meaning of Christ's sacrifice in the New Testament.
